evaluated.name: Distressed external financing intensity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(oancf, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Gross external capital raised (equity plus long-term debt issuance) is benign for healthy firms but signals forced, dilutive survival funding when leverage is high and internal cash generation is weak; the market underweights how expensive this capital is for distressed issuers.
evaluated.reasoning: The financing channel (sstk + dltis scaled by assets) is amplified by a two-part distress rank combining liability burden and operating cash-flow weakness, so the signal only becomes large when issuance coincides with genuine financing pressure. For solvent, cash-generating firms the distress weight collapses and the signal is near zero, isolating the interaction rather than the level of issuance.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Self-funded deleveraging under leverage stress
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at), INDICATOR(RATIO(oancf, at), 0)), INDICATOR(RATIO(lt, at), 0.65))
evaluated.hypothesis: Net long-term debt retirement financed by positive operating cash flow at highly levered firms reveals a credible balance-sheet repair path and declining default probability, which is priced with a lag.
evaluated.reasoning: The double indicator restricts the repayment signal to firms that are both levered (lt/at above 0.65) and internally cash-generating, distinguishing voluntary deleveraging from distressed asset-sale repayment. Unlike a pure repayment signal, the mechanism requires the joint state of high liabilities and positive internal funding, so it captures recovery quality rather than debt flow per se.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Chronic-loss financing dependence
evaluated.expression: MUL(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(ADD(prstkc, dltr), dvt)), at), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(ib), 0), 3))
evaluated.hypothesis: Net external financing raised by firms with a persistent multi-year loss record measures dependence on capital markets for survival; the longer the loss streak, the more each dollar raised reflects deferred failure rather than expansion, predicting negative abnormal returns.
evaluated.reasoning: The financing leg is a full net-external-finance flow (issuance minus repayments, buybacks and dividends), while the distress leg is a persistence count of loss years over three years, so the signal scales with both the amount and the chronicity of dependence. A single bad year earns weight 1 and a three-year loss streak weight 3, encoding the economic idea that repeated recourse to external funding by chronic losers is progressively worse news.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Payout revision under solvency stress
evaluated.expression: MUL(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dvt, prstkc), at), 1), SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Changes in total payout are far more informative about a firm's true financial condition when liabilities are heavy and retained earnings are depleted: a distressed firm that raises distributions is credibly signalling that cash flows can service its debt, while a distressed firm that cuts distributions is conserving liquidity ahead of deteriorating solvency.
evaluated.reasoning: The financing leg is now a signed first difference in payout yield (dividends plus repurchases over assets), so it is not mechanically an inverse-cash proxy and its sign follows the classic positive payout-signalling direction rather than fighting it. The distress leg (leverage plus retained-earnings deficit ranks) acts purely as an information-weight: identical payout revisions at unlevered, profit-rich firms receive near-zero weight, so the predictive content comes from the interaction rather than from the payout level anomaly.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Equity-tilted financing mix with exhausted debt capacity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RATIO(sstk, ADD(sstk, dltis)), SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(ib, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms that tap external capital, the share raised as equity rather than debt reveals whether debt capacity still exists; a distressed, unprofitable firm forced to fund itself with equity has effectively been shut out of credit markets, and such pecking-order inversion predicts poor subsequent returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike the share-issuance anomaly, the financing variable is a composition ratio (equity share of gross external finance) that is scale-free and orthogonal to how much total capital is raised, so it is not a dilution proxy. It only carries adverse information when combined with high liabilities and weak earnings, where equity reliance signals lender rationing rather than opportunistic timing; for healthy firms the same mix is a normal capital-structure choice and receives little weight.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Continuous coverage-weighted deleveraging
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at), 2), MUL(RANK(RATIO(lt, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Net long-term debt retirement is good news in proportion to how levered the firm is and how well operating cash flow covers its liabilities: high-coverage, high-leverage repayers are genuinely repairing solvency, while the same repayment by an unlevered firm is uninformative.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-0 conditional version produced FMB t=+3.1 but only 2% alpha because two hard indicators set the signal to exactly zero for most firms, leaving a thin and unstable long leg. Replacing the 0.65 leverage cutoff and the sign indicator with a product of continuous leverage and cash-flow-coverage ranks preserves the identical economic state (levered but internally funded deleveraging) while giving every firm a graded weight, which should widen the sorted spread without diluting the mechanism.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Debt-funded burn by chronic losers
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at), 2), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(ib), 0), 3))
evaluated.hypothesis: For firms with a multi-year loss record, incremental reliance on new borrowing rather than repayment adds fixed claims to a shrinking earnings base and raises default risk, predicting negative abnormal returns; the equity-issuance component of the same net-financing measure carries very different (timing/option-value) information.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-0 chronic-loss signal mixed equity and debt flows and produced contradictory evidence (FMB t=−3.1 but a positive FF5 alpha), which is what one expects if loss-making equity issuers are high-beta, high-upside names while loss-making borrowers are the genuinely fragile group. Restricting the financing leg to net long-term debt issuance, still weighted by the three-year loss-streak count, is a decomposition test that should align the cross-sectional and portfolio evidence and tell us which flow carries the distress interaction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Forced equity issuance without a liquidity buffer
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(sstk, at), 2), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Equity issuance is precautionary and value-neutral when a firm already holds ample cash and working capital, but is a forced, deeply discounted sale of ownership when the firm has no liquidity buffer against current obligations; only the latter predicts low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This changes the distress axis from solvency/profitability (leverage, losses, cash flow — used in signals 1–4) to a pure short-term liquidity axis, so it tests whether the issuance penalty is driven by insolvency risk or by bargaining weakness at the moment of sale. Because the weights are non-negative liquidity-shortfall ranks, cash-rich issuers fall near zero and the spread is identified by illiquid issuers, a group not isolated by any archive signal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Financing escalation into deteriorating coverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 1), 2), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(oancf, lt), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters is not the level of external capital raised but an escalation of market recourse occurring exactly as internal debt-service capacity deteriorates: firms stepping up issuance while cash-flow-to-liabilities coverage falls are funding a widening gap rather than an opportunity set, and their equity subsequently underperforms.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the level-times-distress-rank template of the archive signal and instead pairs a *change* in financing dependence with a *change* in fundamental coverage, so the identification comes from co-movement of deterioration rather than from the static distressed-issuer penalty. The distress leg is a non-negative rank of coverage deterioration, so the sign is carried entirely by the financing acceleration and firms with improving coverage receive near-zero weight, which keeps the interaction interpretable and the sort stable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Credit-funded distributions with weak debt coverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dvt, prstkc), at), 2), MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, lt)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Distributions are informative about quality only when they are paid out of internal cash flow; when a firm simultaneously raises net new debt and has weak operating-cash-flow coverage of its liabilities, the same distribution is a transfer from creditors to shareholders that cannot be sustained and predicts negative abnormal returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This does not contradict the payout-yield anomaly, because the anomaly concerns cash returned from internal resources, whereas the double rank weighting isolates payouts funded by fresh borrowing at firms whose cash flow barely covers their liability stock — a funding-source interaction rather than a payout-size effect. Both weights are non-negative and continuous, so self-funded payers and low-leverage payers collapse toward zero while the extreme long-short leg is populated by the economically specific "borrow-to-distribute" group.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Net shareholder cash stance under distress
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dvt, prstkc), sstk), at), 2), SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(oancf, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among financially strained firms, the direction of net equity cash flow is the sharpest available statement about true condition: distressed firms returning cash on net reveal viable cash generation, while distressed firms absorbing cash on net reveal dependence on outside capital; the spread between them is mispriced.
evaluated.reasoning: The critique of the earlier certification signal was that a near-binary payer count multiplied by a non-negative distress rank simply reproduces the distress sort; replacing it with signed net shareholder yield (dividends plus repurchases minus equity issuance) gives the financing leg full two-sided cross-sectional variation, so the distress rank only scales an already-informative sign. This also unifies the payout and issuance channels into one testable statement — under distress, cash-returning firms beat cash-absorbing firms — while signal 2 separately tests that the *source* of that cash (new credit) reverses the conclusion.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Within-industry issuance under liquidity shortfall
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: If distressed issuance is genuinely informative, a firm raising unusually much capital relative to its own industry peers while lacking a liquidity buffer should underperform; if instead the effect is an industry-composition artifact (cash-burning biotech and mining versus utilities), within-industry ranking will destroy it.
evaluated.reasoning: Both large-alpha archive signals load on gross issuance, a variable whose level differs by an order of magnitude across sectors, so the long-short portfolio may simply be long capital-hungry industries and short mature ones with the FF5 factors failing to absorb that tilt. Industry-demeaning the financing leg while keeping the liquidity-stress weight is the cleanest available falsification test, and a surviving alpha would substantially raise confidence in the mechanism.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Serial dilution with chronic cash shortfall
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Repeated recourse to the equity market across several years, in a firm whose cash and operating cash flow are both small relative to current liabilities, identifies a business that survives only by serial dilution; the market underestimates the cumulative cost of this dependence.
evaluated.reasoning: Single-year issuance conflates a one-off opportunistic offering with a habitual funding model, and the archive has only tested one-year flows on the equity side; cumulating three years of sstk shifts the concept from an event to a regime. The distress weight also switches to two flow-versus-current-liability coverage measures, so both legs describe chronic states rather than annual shocks, which should reduce turnover and stabilize the portfolio.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: External financing against shrinking revenue
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(sale, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Raising outside capital while the top line is contracting means new money is funding a declining business rather than expansion; such financing signals defensive cash needs and predicts negative abnormal returns, whereas identical financing by a growing firm is investment-driven and benign.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive signal has conditioned on balance-sheet or cash-flow distress (leverage, losses, liquidity), never on operating deterioration, so revenue decline is a genuinely new distress axis and one that is measured with high coverage and little accounting discretion. Both legs are rank-uniform, addressing the skewness problem identified above, and the interaction is economically sharp: it separates growth financing from decline financing without using any leverage variable at all.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Proceeds consumed rather than banked
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sstk, at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The information in an equity offering depends on where the money goes: proceeds that show up as a larger cash balance indicate precautionary or opportunistic financing, whereas proceeds that vanish within the same year — cash falls despite issuance — reveal that the firm was covering an operating or debt-service hole, which predicts low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a use-of-proceeds interaction rather than an amount-of-financing interaction, so it discriminates between two firms with identical issuance and identical leverage, something no archive signal does. It also explains why the issuance-distress alpha might be tail-concentrated: the truly bad group is not all illiquid issuers but the subset whose cash position still deteriorated after raising capital.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Equity raised to repay creditors under weak coverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(sstk, at), 2), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), lt), 0.02)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: When a firm with weak operating-cash-flow coverage of its liabilities sells equity in the same year that it is net retiring debt, the proceeds are effectively transferred to creditors rather than invested; classic debt-overhang logic implies most of the value created accrues to the senior claim, so the shares underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the "issuance level times liquidity rank" family entirely and instead identifies a specific joint financing configuration — simultaneous equity inflow and net debt outflow — which no archive signal isolates and which cannot be produced by either the share-issuance or the debt-financing anomaly alone. The indicator restricts attention to firms retiring at least 2% of their liability stock, so non-issuers and refinancers take the value zero rather than a tie-broken rank, avoiding the degeneracy the critic identified, while the coverage rank supplies the distress conditioning that makes the wealth transfer economically consequential.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sustained deleveraging program with accumulated deficit
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(dltr, dltis), 3), lt)), SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A multi-year program of net debt retirement, measured against the liability stock, is a regime of balance-sheet repair rather than a single financing transaction; for firms carrying heavy liabilities and an accumulated earnings deficit, completing several consecutive years of debt reduction reveals durable cash generation and falling default risk that the market prices only gradually.
evaluated.reasoning: Cumulating three years of net retirement converts the annual debt-flow variable — which is what the known debt-financing anomaly and FF5's investment factor already span — into a persistence/regime measure, the mirror image of the serial-dilution concept on the short side, and one no archive signal has tested. The distress conditioning is restored and strengthened by using accumulated retained-earnings deficit alongside leverage, so the long leg is specifically firms with a damaged equity history that are visibly working their way out, rather than simply profitable low-debt firms that RMW would absorb.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Issuance frequency under chronic shortfall
evaluated.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(sstk, at), 0.05), 5), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What identifies a firm that lives off the capital market is how often it must return, not how much it raised in any single trip; counting years with a material (>5% of assets) equity raise over five years measures habitual dependence and should predict low returns among firms without liquidity buffers.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates one design dimension relative to signals 1 and 2 — frequency versus magnitude — and a count is immune to the extreme right-skew that has repeatedly killed the FMB slope for dollar-based issuance measures. It also naturally down-weights the single large opportunistic offering by a healthy-but-illiquid firm, which is the most plausible source of noise in the winning signal's short leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cumulative issuance against an operating cash-burn streak
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(oancf), 0), 3))
evaluated.hypothesis: The distress state that makes repeated issuance ominous is a persistent inability to generate operating cash, not the level of cash or working capital: firms funding three consecutive years of negative operating cash flow with new equity are financing an unproven business model and underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Every version of the winning mechanism so far conditions on liquidity *stocks* (che/lct, wcap/at) or contemporaneous coverage ratios; substituting a three-year cash-burn streak tests whether the moderator should be a flow-persistence state instead, and unlike the gen-0 accounting-loss streak it uses cash rather than accruals, which explains why that earlier version gave contradictory FMB and alpha signs. Both legs are now regime measures, which should further reduce turnover and stabilize portfolio composition.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Forced debt repayment without liquidity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltr, at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Large gross long-term debt retirements by a firm with no cash buffer and negative working capital are not voluntary deleveraging but mandatory amortization that consumes scarce liquidity, so the same repayment that signals recovery for a liquid firm signals a funding squeeze for an illiquid one.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has only tested *net* debt retirement, which conflates voluntary deleveraging with the repayment leg of a refinancing, and always with a positive expected sign; using gross dltr with a liquidity-shortfall weight tests the opposite economic reading and explains why the net-repayment signals produced solid FMB slopes but no alpha — the two subgroups have opposite return implications and cancel in the extremes.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Paying dividends while selling stock
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(MIN(RATIO(sstk, at), RATIO(dvt, at)), 2), RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Simultaneously distributing cash to shareholders and raising fresh equity is internally inconsistent financing; when operating cash flow is weak relative to current liabilities, it indicates a management unwilling to cut a dividend it cannot fund and financing the shortfall by selling shares, which predicts low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: The MIN operator isolates exactly the overlap of the two flows, so the variable is non-zero only for the specific round-tripping configuration and cannot be reproduced by either the payout-yield or the share-issuance anomaly separately — a genuinely new interaction for this archive. Conditioning on weak cash-flow coverage supplies the distress mechanism (an unfundable dividend commitment), and this also resolves the earlier sign ambiguity about payouts under distress by testing the funding source rather than the payout level.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Burn rate against post-issuance resources
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(oancf), 0), WINSOR(RATIO(ABS(oancf), ADD(che, sstk)), 2))
evaluated.hypothesis: For a firm consuming cash in operations, the relevant distress measure is how fast it burns relative to the resources it actually has after this year's fundraising: a high burn-to-resources ratio means the runway is short and another dilutive raise is imminent, which predicts low returns, whereas a firm that raised many years of burn is not under financing pressure.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not an issuance-magnitude signal at all — equity raised enters the denominator as a resource that relieves pressure, so two firms with identical issuance rank differently depending on their burn, which inverts the direction in which sstk enters relative to the entire archive and to the net-share-issuance anomaly. The indicator confines the measure to cash-burning firms, where the runway concept is economically defined, and the ratio combines a financing flow with two distress variables in a single non-separable quantity rather than a product of a financing leg and a distress weight.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Own-history issuance peak at a liquidity trough
evaluated.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(sstk, at), 5), TS_RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: Financing behaviour is informative relative to a firm's own norm: a firm tapping the equity market at the highest rate of its last five years precisely when its cash-to-current-liabilities position is at its five-year worst is raising capital under duress, and this within-firm coincidence predicts negative abnormal returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Both legs are firm-relative percentiles rather than cross-sectional levels, so the construct is orthogonal by design to the published net-share-issuance and composite-issuance anomalies, which are level effects, and it also sidesteps the split/stock-dividend contamination that made share-count growth unusable. Economically it captures timing coincidence — the worst moment in a firm's own liquidity history is when it is issuing most — which no archive signal measures, and the bounded uniform legs keep both the FMB slope and the sorted portfolios well behaved.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Multi-year amortization burden without liquidity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(dltr, 3), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that have had to hand large sums back to long-term creditors year after year while holding no liquidity buffer are servicing a mandatory amortization schedule out of scarce resources, a sustained funding squeeze that the market underprices.
evaluated.reasoning: The single-year gross-repayment version produced the archive's second-largest alpha (−6.3%, t=−4.3) with a zero FMB slope, exactly the pattern that three-year cumulation repaired on the issuance side, so this tests whether the same temporal fix generalizes to the debt channel. It also addresses the critic's worry that annual dltr proxies for maturity structure noise: a three-year sum is a persistent repayment burden rather than one lumpy maturity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dividend retrenchment by illiquid payers
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(INDICATOR(LAG(dvc, 1), 0), NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(dvc, at), 1), 2))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Because the priced bad state in this archive is forced external financing by illiquid firms, an illiquid dividend payer that cuts its distribution is pre-emptively removing the need to dilute; such retrenchment should be followed by positive abnormal returns, while an illiquid payer that maintains or raises the dividend is heading toward a forced raise.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the archive's first genuinely long-side hypothesis and it is derived from the accumulated evidence rather than from generic payout priors: the mechanism is avoided dilution, not signalling. The prior-payer indicator removes the large mass of non-payers whose zero change would otherwise dominate the ranks, so cross-sectional variation comes from actual payout revisions among firms where liquidity is genuinely scarce.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Gross capital-market turnover under liquidity stress
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(ADD(ADD(sstk, dltis), dltr), 3), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What the archive's separate issuance and repayment findings have in common is dependence on continuous capital-market access; total gross flows through the financing account — equity sold, debt raised, debt retired — measure that dependence directly, and it is costly precisely for firms without a liquidity buffer.
evaluated.reasoning: Gross equity issuance and gross debt repayment, with the same liquidity moderator, produced alphas of −5.1% and −6.3% respectively with opposite conventional interpretations (dilution versus deleveraging), which suggests a common underlying factor of financing turnover rather than two distinct stories. Summing all three gross flows over three years is a decisive test: if turnover is the mechanism, this should dominate both single-channel versions on alpha and slope; if not, it will be visibly diluted, which is equally informative.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dilution that fails to repair the balance sheet
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, at), 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Three years of equity raising should visibly strengthen a firm's working-capital position; when the position has instead deteriorated over exactly the same window, the proceeds were absorbed by operating losses and creditor claims, revealing that the firm is diluting to stand still rather than to invest.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces a *level* moderator (how illiquid the firm is now) with an *efficacy* moderator (whether the money improved the liquidity position over the same horizon as the financing measure), so two equally illiquid serial issuers are separated by whether their financing is working — a distinction no archive signal makes. It also fixes the horizon mismatch that plagued gen-2's "proceeds consumed rather than banked" (one-year change in cash against one-year issuance produced a slope but no alpha) by matching a three-year flow to a three-year state change.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Committed outflows against available resources
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltr, dvt), ADD(act, oancf)), 2)
evaluated.hypothesis: Debt amortization and dividends are quasi-committed cash outflows; their burden is defined only relative to the liquid resources and internal cash generation available to meet them, and firms whose committed outflows are large relative to current assets plus operating cash flow are one shock away from a forced raise or a cut.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike the flagged single-variable ratio, both numerator and denominator are cross-theme composites, so the quantity cannot be reproduced by any issuance or payout anomaly: identical repayment-plus-dividend obligations rank very differently depending on the resource base, which is precisely the interaction. The denominator combines a large, always-positive stock (current assets) with the operating flow, avoiding the small-denominator instability of cash-only or working-capital-deficit scalings, and it unifies the archive's two independently strong channels (gross repayment, payout under stress) into one economically interpretable burden measure.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Net debt build-up by illiquid firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(dltis, dltr), 3), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms without a liquidity buffer that have levered up on net over three consecutive years are adding fixed claims they cannot service from current resources, so sustained net borrowing under illiquidity should predict low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Under the liquidity moderator the archive has tested gross equity issuance (alpha −5.1%) and gross debt repayment (alpha −6.3%) but never the *net* debt flow, and the two gross results have opposite conventional signs, so this is the decisive discriminating test: if capital-market turnover is the mechanism, net borrowing will be uninformative, whereas if leverage accumulation under illiquidity is the mechanism, this signal should be strongly negative on both metrics. The three-year cumulation supplies the regime framing that has repeatedly been what generates a cross-sectional slope in this archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Purified dilution-illiquidity interaction
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The return penalty is specific to the joint state of repeated equity raising and inability to cover current liabilities; once the issuance leg is centered, the signal is high only for illiquid heavy diluters and low for illiquid firms that do not dilute, so any surviving spread is attributable to the interaction rather than to illiquidity alone.
evaluated.reasoning: Centering the financing rank makes the product a textbook interaction term with zero conditional mean for every moderator level, which removes exactly the distress main effect that gen-4 showed was producing near-identical alphas for four contradictory financing legs. If the mechanism is real this should retain both the slope and a substantial alpha; if the alpha collapses, we will have learned that the entire family was a distress-anomaly repackaging — either outcome is decisive for the remaining generations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dilution measured against pre-issuance size
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), LAG(at, 3))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cumulative issuance divided by current assets understates dependence for the heaviest diluters because the proceeds themselves inflate the denominator; scaling three years of equity raised by the asset base that existed before the raises measures how much the firm has been rebuilt with outside money, which is the economically relevant quantity.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a mechanical bias fix rather than a restatement: a firm that tripled its asset base with equity gets a ratio near 0.7 under current-asset scaling but near 2 under pre-issuance scaling, so the ordering of the most dependent firms changes materially. Because the archive's best joint evidence comes from this leg, sharpening its measurement is the highest-value refinement available, and the moderator is held identical so attribution is unambiguous.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Serial dilution with an accumulated earnings deficit
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that keeps selling equity while its retained earnings remain deeply negative has funded a cumulative history of value destruction with outside capital; this stock-of-losses state, rather than current liquidity, may be the distress condition that makes repeated dilution predictive.
evaluated.reasoning: Retained-earnings deficit has only ever been paired with single-year payout or net-debt legs in this archive, never with the multi-year issuance leg that generates the slopes, and unlike liquidity ratios it is a slow-moving cumulative state that should produce low turnover and stable portfolios. It also serves as a moderator-substitution test for signals 1 and 3: if the effect persists across two very different distress states, the mechanism is about dependence on external equity rather than about any single distress proxy.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Repurchases by cash-constrained firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(prstkc, 3), at))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Sustained buybacks are hardest to fake precisely where cash is scarce, so an illiquid firm that has repurchased stock for three years is revealing management's private confidence and unrecognized cash-generating capacity, and its equity should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Repurchases have never been the financing leg in this archive's winning family, and centering the leg means the moderator amplifies both tails symmetrically instead of imposing its own negative main effect — the flaw that doomed every previous positive-sign proposal built on this moderator. It is the natural mirror of signal 1 and provides the long-side evidence the archive still lacks.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Within-deficit-group dilution contrast
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at))), INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(wcap, at)), 0))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms whose current liabilities already exceed their current assets, heavy serial diluters should underperform their non-diluting peers in the same working-capital-deficit condition, while firms with positive working capital are simply uninformative for this mechanism.
evaluated.reasoning: Centering the issuance rank before applying the sample gate places untreated (positive working capital) firms at exactly the middle of the cross-section rather than at the bottom, so the long and short extremes are both drawn from the working-capital-deficit group — the genuine within-group contrast the critic showed the previous version failed to deliver. The tie block is now neutral for the Fama-MacBeth slope as well, since the zero values sit at the conditional mean of the regressor.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Diluting firms with cash-poor earnings
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Serial equity issuers whose reported income substantially exceeds operating cash flow are presenting accrual-supported earnings around their offerings; the gap signals both weak underlying cash generation and incentives to flatter results before raising capital, so subsequent returns should be especially poor.
evaluated.reasoning: The earnings–cash-flow divergence is a distress axis this archive has never used, and it is conceptually distinct from every liquidity, leverage, loss-streak or retained-earnings moderator tested so far: it measures the credibility of reported performance rather than the level of financial strain. It supplies a specific reason why the market fails to discount repeated dilution promptly — the accounting looks acceptable at the time of the raise — and both legs are rank-uniform with high coverage, which is the configuration that has produced sign-consistent slopes in this archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Equity raised per dollar of pre-period revenue
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), LAG(sale, 3))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Dependence on outside equity is best expressed relative to the operating scale the firm actually runs — a company that has raised two years of revenue from shareholders is living on investor capital regardless of how large its balance sheet has become — and this dependence is priced most sharply when current liabilities cannot be covered.
evaluated.reasoning: Assets are the direct destination of issuance proceeds, so even a lagged asset base is partly endogenous to the financing history, whereas revenue is a genuinely independent measure of operating scale; this makes the denominator choice an economic refinement rather than a rescaling. Sale-based scaling also keeps the deep-burn, pre-revenue diluters at the informative extreme instead of compressing them, which is where the mechanism should be strongest.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dilution during active erosion of retained earnings
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(re, at), 4))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters is not the accumulated stock of past losses but whether the deficit is still deepening: firms selling equity while retained earnings are on a declining four-year path are funding losses that are actively continuing, whereas firms with an old, stable deficit may already be recovering.
evaluated.reasoning: The retained-earnings *level* moderator produced a good slope (−2.11) but a wrong-signed alpha (+3.8%), which is what one expects if deep-deficit firms are a stable, heavily factor-loaded group whose distress is already in prices; replacing the level with its trend isolates ongoing deterioration and should restore sign agreement between the two metrics. This distinguishes a flow-of-deficit state from a stock-of-deficit state, a distinction no archive signal has drawn.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Lender-certified versus unscreened funding under illiquidity
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(dltis, 3), ADD(TS_SUM(dltis, 3), TS_SUM(sstk, 3))))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among illiquid firms that must raise outside capital, those able to fund themselves with long-term debt have passed a lender's credit screen and possess verifiable collateral and cash flow, whereas those forced to fund with equity have not; the debt-funded group should outperform the equity-funded group.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a new economic hypothesis — certification by informed creditors — rather than another dependence measure, and the centered mix leg means the moderator amplifies both tails symmetrically so the sign is carried by the funding composition rather than by illiquidity itself, the flaw that sank earlier long-side attempts. The gen-0 mix test was single-year, uncentered and paired with a solvency moderator, so this is a substantively different specification of a previously inconclusive idea.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dilution by firms with no taxable income
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(txt, sale))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Tax expense is the hardest-to-manipulate evidence that a firm actually earns money; a company that has repeatedly sold equity while paying almost no tax relative to its revenue is pre-profit or loss-making in economic substance, and its dilution therefore funds consumption rather than value creation.
evaluated.reasoning: Tax burden relative to sales is an entirely unused distress axis in this archive and is conceptually distinct from liquidity ratios, accrual gaps and retained-earnings measures because it is validated by an outside party rather than by management's own accounting choices. Holding the champion's financing leg and scaling fixed, this asks whether verified absence of profit is a sharper conditioning state than balance-sheet liquidity, which is a genuine economic question rather than a parameter tweak.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Maturity substitution under illiquidity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), at), RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that increases short-term borrowing while its long-term debt is shrinking on net has been pushed down the maturity ladder by lenders; for a firm that also cannot cover current liabilities from cash or operations, this substitution creates immediate rollover risk that the market prices with a lag.
evaluated.reasoning: Maturity structure has never been validly tested in this archive — the gen-0 attempt failed theme validation — and the construct is economically distinct from every dependence, drain or amortization measure evaluated so far because it holds total borrowing roughly fixed and looks only at its composition. The leg is signed and two-sided (firms terming out debt sit at the opposite extreme from firms compressing maturity), which is the configuration that has produced cross-sectional slopes here, and the liquidity moderator supplies the state in which rollover risk actually binds.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Shareholder-funded share of cash inflows
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), ADD(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), ABS(TS_SUM(oancf, 3))))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The cleanest measure of external dependence is the fraction of a firm's three-year cash inflows that came from selling shares rather than from operations; a firm near the top of that fraction is run on investor money, and this is most damaging where current obligations exceed current resources.
evaluated.reasoning: This is self-normalizing — the financing flow is divided by the sum of itself and internally generated cash, so it is bounded in [0,1] and needs no external scaler at all, which removes the denominator-endogeneity problem the champion attacked with a lagged asset base while requiring no extra year of history and therefore not compressing coverage further. Using the absolute value of cumulative operating cash flow keeps cash-burning firms interpretable (their burn magnitude, not its sign, measures the alternative funding they lack), making the ratio a genuine cross-theme construct rather than a scaled issuance measure.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Equity funding an operating working-capital bloat
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), RANK(GROWTH(RATIO(SUB(act, che), sale), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: When a serial equity issuer's non-cash current assets are growing faster than its sales, the money raised is being absorbed by uncollected receivables and unsold inventory rather than by productive investment, which signals deteriorating operations and the likelihood of further dilution.
evaluated.reasoning: Operating working-capital efficiency is an entirely new distress axis for this archive and it is conceptually independent of the funding-capacity ratios that have dominated: it asks where the money went in the operating cycle, not whether obligations can be met. It also gives a specific, testable use-of-proceeds mechanism that the earlier one-year change-in-cash test could not capture, since inventory and receivable bloat is exactly how proceeds disappear without cash ever appearing on the balance sheet.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Internal coverage of debt amortization under illiquidity
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(oancf, 3), TS_SUM(dltr, 3)), 2))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms with no liquidity buffer, those whose three-year operating cash flow comfortably covers the debt they have had to repay are servicing their obligations from the business itself and are far less fragile than their balance sheets suggest, so they should earn positive abnormal returns relative to illiquid firms that cannot cover amortization internally.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the archive's first long-side construct built on debt-service capacity rather than on payout behaviour, and centering the leg means the illiquidity moderator amplifies both tails symmetrically instead of imposing its own negative main effect — the defect that sank the earlier repurchase and dividend-retrenchment tests. It directly complements signal 1: one measures dependence on shareholders, the other self-sufficiency against creditors, and together they establish whether the mechanism is symmetric or purely short-side.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Serial dilution with near-term debt overhang
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, act)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that has repeatedly sold equity and also carries debt maturing within the year that is large relative to its entire current asset base faces a hard deadline: the next repayment must be met from a new raise, so its bargaining position with investors is at its weakest and returns should be poor.
evaluated.reasoning: Every moderator tested so far measures obligations in aggregate (current liabilities, working capital, cash flow coverage); this one measures the *maturity* of the claim that is about to come due against liquid resources, which is the specific state that forces dilution on the issuer's terms rather than the firm's. Both legs are stable, always-positive ratios with no sign-flip or blow-up risk, and the debt-overhang leg is not a rescaling of anything in the archive, so the test is about a new distress state rather than a new denominator.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dependence meeting a fresh collapse in funding capacity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(che, oancf), lct), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A history of dilution becomes actionable news when funding capacity suddenly deteriorates: firms whose cash-plus-operating-flow coverage of current liabilities has just fallen sharply are the ones about to return to the market, and the timing of that deterioration is what the market is slow to price.
evaluated.reasoning: This pairs a slow-moving dependence state with a one-year shock to funding capacity rather than with another level of distress, so it tests timing rather than intensity — an axis on which the archive has only one weak observation (gen-1's one-year financing escalation against coverage deterioration, which used a noisy one-year financing leg). Because the shock leg is a signed change while the dependence leg is a cumulative state, the two legs carry genuinely different information and neither is a monotone transform of any evaluated signal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Self-funding ratio under liquidity stress
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(oancf, 3), ADD(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), TS_SUM(dltis, 3))), 2))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms whose balance sheets look strained, those that generated far more cash internally than they raised from equity and debt markets over three years are only nominally distressed, and the market's failure to distinguish them from genuinely market-dependent firms creates positive abnormal returns.
evaluated.reasoning: The ratio of internal cash generation to total external capital raised is a single non-separable quantity spanning both themes and both external channels, and it is not the inverse of any tested leg because no archive signal has placed operating cash flow in the numerator against combined equity-and-debt issuance. Centering the leg lets the illiquidity moderator amplify both tails symmetrically, which is the only construction in this archive that has ever allowed a sign to be carried by the financing variable rather than by the distress main effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cumulative equity funding gap under liquidity deficit
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), TS_SUM(oancf, 3)), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: External dependence should be measured net of what the business produced: raising a lot while also generating cash is not dependence, whereas raising a lot while burning cash is a true funding gap, and such gaps are most dangerous for firms whose working capital is already negative.
evaluated.reasoning: The signed numerator is the substantive idea — it separates opportunistic issuers from cash-consuming ones, a distinction no evaluated signal makes since gen-0's single-year net-financing test was dominated by payout terms and a loss-streak multiplier — and scaling by total assets removes the sign-flipping denominator the critic identified while keeping severe gaps at the extreme. Pairing it with the wcap-inclusive moderator, which has produced the archive's largest alphas, targets the joint objective directly.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Funding gap facing a refinancing deadline
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), TS_SUM(oancf, 3)), at)), SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, act), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The sharpest measure of dependence is equity raised net of cash generated internally over the same three years, and such a gap is most dangerous for a firm that must refinance maturing debt out of a depleted current asset base.
evaluated.reasoning: The gap leg produced the archive's largest alpha (−7.0%) but no slope, while the deadline channel produced the largest slope; pairing them tests directly whether the slope deficiency of the gap leg was a moderator problem rather than a leg problem. The numerator is signed so opportunistic issuers who also generate cash sit at the opposite extreme from cash-burning issuers, which is the economic distinction the pure issuance legs cannot make.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Distributions ahead of maturing debt
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(dvt, 3), at)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, act)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Paying out cash for three consecutive years while carrying short-term debt that is large relative to current assets means the firm has prioritized shareholders over an approaching refinancing; the payout is not evidence of strength but of an obligation the board is unwilling to cut before the deadline binds.
evaluated.reasoning: The payout channel has repeatedly failed in this archive when conditioned on liquidity stocks or coverage flows, but it has never been conditioned on maturity timing, which is the state where a distribution genuinely competes with a repayment. Because the newly validated deadline channel supplies the slope, this is the most promising remaining specification of the payout-drain mechanism and it is economically distinct from the dilution family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dilution with a short maturity ladder and weak internal coverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dlc, dltt)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A serial diluter is most vulnerable when its debt is overwhelmingly short-dated in composition and its operating cash flow cannot cover current obligations: the maturity mix sets how often it must face lenders, and the cash-flow shortfall determines whether it can survive a refusal.
evaluated.reasoning: The first channel is now maturity *composition* (share of debt due within a year), which is scale-free and therefore not the same information as dlc/act or wcap/at — a highly levered firm and an almost debt-free firm can both be entirely short-dated — so the critic's mechanical-overlap objection no longer applies. The second channel is a cash-flow coverage measure rather than another balance-sheet stock, so the two conditioning dimensions are structure and servicing capacity rather than two versions of short-term liquidity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unfunded near-term maturities
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(dlc, ADD(che, ADD(sstk, dltis))), 2)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The relevant question for a firm with debt coming due is whether cash on hand plus the capital it actually managed to raise this year covers that obligation; when maturities dwarf cash-plus-new-funding and operating cash flow cannot cover current liabilities, another raise on worse terms is inevitable.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a scaled issuance measure — equity and debt raised enter the denominator as resources that *relieve* the obligation, so the same issuance that makes the archive's dilution signals bearish makes this measure less negative, which is the opposite direction and cannot be a leverage double-count. The construct combines a financing flow with a maturity stock and a liquidity stock in one non-separable quantity, and the denominator is a sum of non-negative items, avoiding the sign-flip and blow-up problems flagged earlier.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Issuance while funding capacity is intact
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RATIO(sstk, at), 0.03), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ADD(che, oancf), lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Equity issuance is not intrinsically bad news: among firms that actually raise material equity, those doing so with ample cash and operating cash flow relative to current liabilities are timing a favourable window from a position of strength and should outperform those raising because they have run out of resources.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than asserting a self-sufficiency sign that the archive's evidence contradicts, this takes the archive's one robust finding — issuance is penalized *when* funding capacity is absent — and tests its logical complement within the treated group, so the hypothesis is disciplined by prior results instead of fighting them. Centering the capacity rank before the issuance gate places non-issuers at the middle of the cross-section, so both extremes are populated by issuers and the sort is a genuine within-issuer contrast.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dilution as the maturity burden worsens
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, act), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: For a firm dependent on equity markets, what matters is not only that near-term debt is large relative to liquid assets but that this burden has just deteriorated: a sharp increase in maturing debt relative to current assets signals that creditors have shortened terms or that liquid assets have been consumed, forcing the next raise sooner.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has established the *level* of the maturity burden as its strongest conditioning variable (fmb −3.51) but never tested its change, and the level-versus-trend distinction has previously produced materially different results here (retained-earnings level versus trend gave opposite-signed alphas). A one-year deterioration is also a timing variable, so if it carries the effect we learn that the mechanism is about newly arriving pressure rather than a chronic state — a substantive economic distinction rather than an operator swap.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Forward external funding requirement
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(MUL(NEG(oancf), INDICATOR(NEG(oancf), 0)), ADD(dlc, dltr)), che), at), 2)
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically primitive quantity in this whole research line is how much cash a firm must obtain from outside in the near term: its operating burn if it is burning, plus debt coming due and the amortization it is currently paying, less the cash it holds. Firms with a large positive requirement must transact with the market on unfavourable terms and underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the archive's leg-times-moderator template with one integrated cash-requirement identity in which the financing claims (maturing and amortizing debt) and the distress terms (floored burn, cash holdings) are inseparable — no ranking of one leg by another. The burn term is properly floored using MUL(NEG(oancf), INDICATOR(NEG(oancf), 0)) so cash-generating firms contribute zero burn rather than being misclassified, which is the exact defect the critic identified in the survival-horizon expression.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Serial dilution with a thin equity cushion
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ceq, at)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Repeated equity raising is most damaging when the book equity cushion absorbing losses is already thin and operating cash flow cannot cover current obligations, because each new round is priced against a claim that is close to being wiped out.
evaluated.reasoning: The equity cushion ceq/at has never been used anywhere in this archive — all solvency conditioning went through lt/at, re/at or liquidity ratios — and it is a distinct economic state from short-term liquidity: a firm can hold ample cash yet have almost no equity buffer after years of losses. Pairing it with the cash-flow coverage channel that has generated the archive's reliable slopes gives a coherent solvency-plus-servicing conditioning set rather than another restatement of the maturity/liquidity channels.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Distributions exceeding internal cash generation before maturities
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(dvt, 3), TS_SUM(oancf, 3)), at)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, act)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that has distributed more cash to shareholders over three years than its operations produced, while carrying near-term maturities large relative to its current assets, has funded shareholder payments from borrowings or reserves and is exposed when the debt must be refinanced.
evaluated.reasoning: Expressing affordability as a signed difference scaled by assets eliminates the sign inversion the critic identified in the ratio version — stressed payers with negative cumulative cash flow now score at the top of the distribution, exactly where the hypothesis places them, instead of flipping to the long side. It is also economically distinct from the evaluated payout-level signal because a large dividend paid out of larger cash flow now scores near zero rather than extreme.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Within-deadline-group dilution contrast
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at))), INDICATOR(RATIO(dlc, act), 0.25))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms whose short-term debt exceeds a quarter of their current assets, serial diluters should underperform diluting-free peers facing the same refinancing deadline; for firms without a meaningful near-term maturity the dilution history should carry no penalty.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike MIN aggregation, which the critic correctly notes is nearly rank-equivalent to the product for uniform ranks, a hard gate combined with a centered financing rank places untreated firms at the exact middle of the cross-section so both extremes are drawn from the deadline group — a genuine within-group contrast rather than distressed-versus-undistressed. This design already proved diagnostic when applied to the working-capital-deficit gate, and applying it to the archive's strongest conditioning channel is the sharpest remaining test of whether the interaction, not the distress main effect, carries the return predictability.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Rank-composite dependence under liquidity deficit
evaluated.expression: MUL(SUMRANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at), NEG(RATIO(TS_SUM(oancf, 3), at))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Dependence on outside equity has two components — how much was raised and how little the business generated — and combining them in rank space rather than as a dollar difference should identify dependent firms across the whole cross-section rather than only in the extreme tail.
evaluated.reasoning: The dollar-difference funding gap produced the archive's largest alphas (−6.1% to −7.0%) but a Fama-MacBeth slope of +0.20, the classic signature of a heavily right-skewed regressor whose information sits entirely in the tail; averaging the two ranked components makes the leg uniform and should convert that tail information into a linear slope while preserving the sorted extremes that generate the alpha. This is a measurement-construction fix aimed precisely at the parent signal's diagnosed weakness, not an industry-adjustment diagnostic that the archive has already answered.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dilution against a floored survival horizon
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, ADD(ADD(MUL(NEG(oancf), INDICATOR(NEG(oancf), 0)), dlc), dltr)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A market-dependent firm's survival horizon is its cash divided by the cash it must actually spend — its operating burn when it burns, plus maturing and amortizing debt; serial diluters with short horizons must return to the market imminently and underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: The burn term is now floored via MUL(NEG(oancf), INDICATOR(NEG(oancf), 0)), so profitable firms contribute zero burn and are scored by their debt obligations alone, repairing the sign contradiction the critic identified while keeping the denominator strictly non-negative. Including scheduled amortization (dltr) alongside maturing short-term debt both completes the obligation measure economically and reduces the incidence of a zero denominator, and no archive signal has expressed the distress state as a horizon in time units rather than a static ratio.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Distressed external financing intensity
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(oancf, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Gross external capital raised (equity plus long-term debt issuance) is benign for healthy firms but signals forced, dilutive survival funding when leverage is high and internal cash generation is weak; the market underweights how expensive this capital is for distressed issuers.
considered.reasoning: The financing channel (sstk + dltis scaled by assets) is amplified by a two-part distress rank combining liability burden and operating cash-flow weakness, so the signal only becomes large when issuance coincides with genuine financing pressure. For solvent, cash-generating firms the distress weight collapses and the signal is near zero, isolating the interaction rather than the level of issuance.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Self-funded deleveraging under leverage stress
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at), INDICATOR(RATIO(oancf, at), 0)), INDICATOR(RATIO(lt, at), 0.65))
considered.hypothesis: Net long-term debt retirement financed by positive operating cash flow at highly levered firms reveals a credible balance-sheet repair path and declining default probability, which is priced with a lag.
considered.reasoning: The double indicator restricts the repayment signal to firms that are both levered (lt/at above 0.65) and internally cash-generating, distinguishing voluntary deleveraging from distressed asset-sale repayment. Unlike a pure repayment signal, the mechanism requires the joint state of high liabilities and positive internal funding, so it captures recovery quality rather than debt flow per se.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Maturity shortening with weak liquidity
considered.expression: MUL(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dlc, dltt)), 1), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
considered.hypothesis: A shift of the debt mix toward short maturities is a rollover-risk event only for firms with little cash relative to current liabilities and negative working capital; such firms face imminent refinancing and covenant pressure that the market prices slowly.
considered.reasoning: The financing component is the annual change in the short-term share of total debt, which captures deliberate or forced maturity shortening independent of leverage level. Weighting it by liquidity-stress ranks (cash-to-current-liabilities and working capital) creates a rollover-risk interaction that vanishes for cash-rich firms.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Chronic-loss financing dependence
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(ADD(prstkc, dltr), dvt)), at), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(ib), 0), 3))
considered.hypothesis: Net external financing raised by firms with a persistent multi-year loss record measures dependence on capital markets for survival; the longer the loss streak, the more each dollar raised reflects deferred failure rather than expansion, predicting negative abnormal returns.
considered.reasoning: The financing leg is a full net-external-finance flow (issuance minus repayments, buybacks and dividends), while the distress leg is a persistence count of loss years over three years, so the signal scales with both the amount and the chronicity of dependence. A single bad year earns weight 1 and a three-year loss streak weight 3, encoding the economic idea that repeated recourse to external funding by chronic losers is progressively worse news.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Payout revision under solvency stress
considered.expression: MUL(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dvt, prstkc), at), 1), SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Changes in total payout are far more informative about a firm's true financial condition when liabilities are heavy and retained earnings are depleted: a distressed firm that raises distributions is credibly signalling that cash flows can service its debt, while a distressed firm that cuts distributions is conserving liquidity ahead of deteriorating solvency.
considered.reasoning: The financing leg is now a signed first difference in payout yield (dividends plus repurchases over assets), so it is not mechanically an inverse-cash proxy and its sign follows the classic positive payout-signalling direction rather than fighting it. The distress leg (leverage plus retained-earnings deficit ranks) acts purely as an information-weight: identical payout revisions at unlevered, profit-rich firms receive near-zero weight, so the predictive content comes from the interaction rather than from the payout level anomaly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Equity-tilted financing mix with exhausted debt capacity
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(sstk, ADD(sstk, dltis)), SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(ib, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Among firms that tap external capital, the share raised as equity rather than debt reveals whether debt capacity still exists; a distressed, unprofitable firm forced to fund itself with equity has effectively been shut out of credit markets, and such pecking-order inversion predicts poor subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: Unlike the share-issuance anomaly, the financing variable is a composition ratio (equity share of gross external finance) that is scale-free and orthogonal to how much total capital is raised, so it is not a dilution proxy. It only carries adverse information when combined with high liabilities and weak earnings, where equity reliance signals lender rationing rather than opportunistic timing; for healthy firms the same mix is a normal capital-structure choice and receives little weight.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Continuous coverage-weighted deleveraging
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at), 2), MUL(RANK(RATIO(lt, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: Net long-term debt retirement is good news in proportion to how levered the firm is and how well operating cash flow covers its liabilities: high-coverage, high-leverage repayers are genuinely repairing solvency, while the same repayment by an unlevered firm is uninformative.
considered.reasoning: The gen-0 conditional version produced FMB t=+3.1 but only 2% alpha because two hard indicators set the signal to exactly zero for most firms, leaving a thin and unstable long leg. Replacing the 0.65 leverage cutoff and the sign indicator with a product of continuous leverage and cash-flow-coverage ranks preserves the identical economic state (levered but internally funded deleveraging) while giving every firm a graded weight, which should widen the sorted spread without diluting the mechanism.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Debt-funded burn by chronic losers
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at), 2), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(ib), 0), 3))
considered.hypothesis: For firms with a multi-year loss record, incremental reliance on new borrowing rather than repayment adds fixed claims to a shrinking earnings base and raises default risk, predicting negative abnormal returns; the equity-issuance component of the same net-financing measure carries very different (timing/option-value) information.
considered.reasoning: The gen-0 chronic-loss signal mixed equity and debt flows and produced contradictory evidence (FMB t=−3.1 but a positive FF5 alpha), which is what one expects if loss-making equity issuers are high-beta, high-upside names while loss-making borrowers are the genuinely fragile group. Restricting the financing leg to net long-term debt issuance, still weighted by the three-year loss-streak count, is a decomposition test that should align the cross-sectional and portfolio evidence and tell us which flow carries the distress interaction.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Forced equity issuance without a liquidity buffer
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(sstk, at), 2), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Equity issuance is precautionary and value-neutral when a firm already holds ample cash and working capital, but is a forced, deeply discounted sale of ownership when the firm has no liquidity buffer against current obligations; only the latter predicts low returns.
considered.reasoning: This changes the distress axis from solvency/profitability (leverage, losses, cash flow — used in signals 1–4) to a pure short-term liquidity axis, so it tests whether the issuance penalty is driven by insolvency risk or by bargaining weakness at the moment of sale. Because the weights are non-negative liquidity-shortfall ranks, cash-rich issuers fall near zero and the spread is identified by illiquid issuers, a group not isolated by any archive signal.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Financing escalation into deteriorating coverage
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 1), 2), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(oancf, lt), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: What matters is not the level of external capital raised but an escalation of market recourse occurring exactly as internal debt-service capacity deteriorates: firms stepping up issuance while cash-flow-to-liabilities coverage falls are funding a widening gap rather than an opportunity set, and their equity subsequently underperforms.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the level-times-distress-rank template of the archive signal and instead pairs a *change* in financing dependence with a *change* in fundamental coverage, so the identification comes from co-movement of deterioration rather than from the static distressed-issuer penalty. The distress leg is a non-negative rank of coverage deterioration, so the sign is carried entirely by the financing acceleration and firms with improving coverage receive near-zero weight, which keeps the interaction interpretable and the sort stable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Credit-funded distributions with weak debt coverage
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dvt, prstkc), at), 2), MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, lt)))))
considered.hypothesis: Distributions are informative about quality only when they are paid out of internal cash flow; when a firm simultaneously raises net new debt and has weak operating-cash-flow coverage of its liabilities, the same distribution is a transfer from creditors to shareholders that cannot be sustained and predicts negative abnormal returns.
considered.reasoning: This does not contradict the payout-yield anomaly, because the anomaly concerns cash returned from internal resources, whereas the double rank weighting isolates payouts funded by fresh borrowing at firms whose cash flow barely covers their liability stock — a funding-source interaction rather than a payout-size effect. Both weights are non-negative and continuous, so self-funded payers and low-leverage payers collapse toward zero while the extreme long-short leg is populated by the economically specific "borrow-to-distribute" group.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Net shareholder cash stance under distress
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dvt, prstkc), sstk), at), 2), SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(oancf, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Among financially strained firms, the direction of net equity cash flow is the sharpest available statement about true condition: distressed firms returning cash on net reveal viable cash generation, while distressed firms absorbing cash on net reveal dependence on outside capital; the spread between them is mispriced.
considered.reasoning: The critique of the earlier certification signal was that a near-binary payer count multiplied by a non-negative distress rank simply reproduces the distress sort; replacing it with signed net shareholder yield (dividends plus repurchases minus equity issuance) gives the financing leg full two-sided cross-sectional variation, so the distress rank only scales an already-informative sign. This also unifies the payout and issuance channels into one testable statement — under distress, cash-returning firms beat cash-absorbing firms — while signal 2 separately tests that the *source* of that cash (new credit) reverses the conclusion.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Within-industry issuance under liquidity shortfall
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
considered.hypothesis: If distressed issuance is genuinely informative, a firm raising unusually much capital relative to its own industry peers while lacking a liquidity buffer should underperform; if instead the effect is an industry-composition artifact (cash-burning biotech and mining versus utilities), within-industry ranking will destroy it.
considered.reasoning: Both large-alpha archive signals load on gross issuance, a variable whose level differs by an order of magnitude across sectors, so the long-short portfolio may simply be long capital-hungry industries and short mature ones with the FF5 factors failing to absorb that tilt. Industry-demeaning the financing leg while keeping the liquidity-stress weight is the cleanest available falsification test, and a surviving alpha would substantially raise confidence in the mechanism.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Serial dilution with chronic cash shortfall
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
considered.hypothesis: Repeated recourse to the equity market across several years, in a firm whose cash and operating cash flow are both small relative to current liabilities, identifies a business that survives only by serial dilution; the market underestimates the cumulative cost of this dependence.
considered.reasoning: Single-year issuance conflates a one-off opportunistic offering with a habitual funding model, and the archive has only tested one-year flows on the equity side; cumulating three years of sstk shifts the concept from an event to a regime. The distress weight also switches to two flow-versus-current-liability coverage measures, so both legs describe chronic states rather than annual shocks, which should reduce turnover and stabilize the portfolio.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: External financing against shrinking revenue
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(sale, 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Raising outside capital while the top line is contracting means new money is funding a declining business rather than expansion; such financing signals defensive cash needs and predicts negative abnormal returns, whereas identical financing by a growing firm is investment-driven and benign.
considered.reasoning: Every archive signal has conditioned on balance-sheet or cash-flow distress (leverage, losses, liquidity), never on operating deterioration, so revenue decline is a genuinely new distress axis and one that is measured with high coverage and little accounting discretion. Both legs are rank-uniform, addressing the skewness problem identified above, and the interaction is economically sharp: it separates growth financing from decline financing without using any leverage variable at all.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Proceeds consumed rather than banked
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sstk, at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: The information in an equity offering depends on where the money goes: proceeds that show up as a larger cash balance indicate precautionary or opportunistic financing, whereas proceeds that vanish within the same year — cash falls despite issuance — reveal that the firm was covering an operating or debt-service hole, which predicts low returns.
considered.reasoning: This is a use-of-proceeds interaction rather than an amount-of-financing interaction, so it discriminates between two firms with identical issuance and identical leverage, something no archive signal does. It also explains why the issuance-distress alpha might be tail-concentrated: the truly bad group is not all illiquid issuers but the subset whose cash position still deteriorated after raising capital.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Equity raised to repay creditors under weak coverage
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(sstk, at), 2), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), lt), 0.02)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, lt))))
